item.title: From 2017 crackdown to UN court, a decade of the Rohingya crisis
item.description:
MYANMAR-ROHINGYA/WORLD COURT

The United Nations' highest court for disputes between states, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), will rule on Thursday in a landmark case accusing Buddhist-majority Myanmar of committing genocide against the minority Rohingyas, who are mostly Muslim.

More than one million Rohingya refugees who fled Myanmar currently live in Bangladesh, most of them in the Cox's Bazar district, according to the UN.

Here is a timeline of events in the Rohingya crisis:

25 Aug, 2017 - The Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), a Muslim militia, attacks 30 police posts and a military base in Myanmar's Rakhine State.

26 Aug, 2017 - Thousands of Rohingya people flee across the border into Bangladesh as clashes between Myanmar's military and ARSA intensify.

2 Sept, 2017 - More than 2,600 houses are razed in Rohingya-majority areas in the week following the 25 August attack according to the Myanmar government.

11 Sept, 2017 - The UN human rights high commissioner calls the military operation "a textbook example of ethnic cleansing".

19 Sept, 2017 - Myanmar leader Aung San Suu Kyi pledges to hold those behind rights abuses to account, but makes no mention of UN accusations of ethnic cleansing.

12 Dec, 2017 - Medecins Sans Frontières publishes survey results from Rohingya refugee camps in Bangladesh that say at least 6,700 Rohingya, in the most conservative estimations, were killed between 25 August and 24 September, including at least 730 children below the age of five years.

10 Jan, 2018 - The military admits its soldiers killed 10 detained Rohingya at Inn Din village. Seven soldiers are sentenced in April 2018 but released early in May 2019.

11 Nov, 2019 – Predominantly Muslim Gambia files a genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of atrocities against the Rohingya.

11 Dec, 2019 - Aung San Suu Kyi appears before the ICJ in The Hague and rejects genocide allegations as "incomplete and misleading."

23 Jan, 2020 – The ICJ orders Myanmar to take urgent measures to protect Rohingya people who remain in the country.

1 Feb, 2021 – Myanmar's military stages a coup, arrests Aung San Suu Kyi and overthrows the elected government, sparking nationwide conflict.

22 July, 2022 – The ICJ rejects objections raised by Myanmar and rules it has jurisdiction under the Genocide Convention and that Gambia's application is admissible.

12 Jan, 2026 - Myanmar targeted minority Muslim Rohingya for destruction and made their lives a nightmare, Gambia tells ICJ judges, as public hearings on the merits of the case begin.

16 Jan, 2026 - Myanmar tells the ICJ that Gambia has not proven the Rohingya genocide case, following a statement by the foreign ministry that terms the allegations by Gambia as "flawed and unfounded in fact and law."

3 Nov, 2026 – The ICJ announces it will deliver its judgment on 19 November.

item.title: City Bank promotes youth entrepreneurship through Bangladesh Bank’s UDYOG initiative in Munshiganj
item.description:
City Bank organised an awareness and stakeholder engagement event in Munshiganj today, Thursday, to promote Bangladesh Bank’s UDYOG (Upazila-Driven Youth Opportunity for Growth) initiative, encouraging aspiring young entrepreneurs to access formal financing and develop sustainable businesses, says a press release.

The programme held at Darbar Party Palace in Munshiganj. Mashrur Arefin, Managing Director & CEO of City Bank was the Chief Guest and Sheikh Abdul Kuddus, Director of the SME & Special Programmes Department (SMESPD), Bangladesh Bank was the Special Guest of this ceremony.

The event was also attended by Mohammad Masudur Rahman, Joint Director, Ashanur Rahman, DMD, Chief Economist & Country Business Manager of City Bank and other officials of City Bank and others Bank. Along with them a diverse group of aspiring young entrepreneurs from across the region and media representatives were also present at the event.

The event highlighted the programme's objectives, eligibility criteria, financing facilities and application process, providing aspiring entrepreneurs with an opportunity to interact directly with Bangladesh Bank officials and banking professionals.

Introduced through Bangladesh Bank's SMESPD Circular, under Section 45 of the Bank Company Act, 1991, UDYOG aims to identify and finance promising young entrepreneurs at the upozila level, addressing barriers such as limited business experience, inadequate collateral and restricted access to institutional financing. Under the programme, selected entrepreneurs can receive blended financing of up to BDT 20 lakh, comprising a bank loan of up to BDT 10 lakh and an equivalent grant of up to BDT 10 lakh, subject to eligibility and applicable guidelines.

The loan component is eligible for refinancing under relevant Bangladesh Bank refinance schemes. Beyond financing, the programme provides financial literacy training, entrepreneurship development, mentoring, assistance with business registration and business plan preparation, and access to market linkages.

During the programme, the Joint Director of SMESPD, Bangladesh Bank, briefed participants on the key aspects of the UDYOG initiative, including its objectives, eligibility requirements, financing structure and implementation framework, offering insights into the opportunities available for aspiring young entrepreneurs. Initially launched across 64 upazilas in eight districts, the programme received 22,000 applications. Following this encouraging response, Bangladesh Bank expanded its coverage to the remaining 56 districts from 1 November 2026.

City Bank has been designated as the Upazila Lead Bank for 12 upazilas: Alfadanga, Gopalganj Sadar, Bhairab, Munshiganj Sadar, Sonargaon, Shibpur, Hajiganj, Laksam, Senbagh, Sirajganj Sadar, Bishwanath and Dinajpur Sadar. The Bank also serves as the District Lead Bank for Gopalganj and Munshiganj, and Joint District Lead Bank for Mymensingh.

In its lead bank capacity, City Bank will coordinate with participating banks and relevant stakeholders. The bank also facilitates application consolidation, forwarding and support the identification and financing of eligible entrepreneurs in accordance with Bangladesh Bank's guidelines. Applicants can submit their applications through any scheduled bank branch in the designated upozilas. The selection process involves transparent screening, independent credit appraisal by the financing banks and simultaneous disbursement of the approved loan and equivalent grant in a 50:50 ratios, followed by monitoring of business progress, fund utilization and loan repayment.

At the event, City Bank also formally launched its dedicated ‘UDYOG’ Loan facility to facilitate financing for eligible young entrepreneurs under the Bangladesh Bank initiative. Through its role as lead bank across designated upazilas and districts, City Bank remains committed to advancing Bangladesh Bank's vision of nurturing youth entrepreneurship, promoting self-employment and fostering inclusive economic growth across the country.

item.title: The silent tax of illiquidity: Why secondary market depth matters
item.description:
In Bangladesh's policy circles, developing vibrant secondary financial markets has been a familiar talking point for some time. Yet, year after year, meaningful market reforms stay near the bottom of the economic agenda. The reason is clear. We often praise the general idea of secondary markets, but we rarely explain the real, everyday damage caused by their absence. When weak trading is seen merely as a minor headache for brokers rather than a major drag on national growth, the urgency to act disappears.

Across Bangladesh's fixed income, currency, and equity markets, we have built entry gates without exits. This lack of easy buying and selling acts as a silent tax on the entire economy. When secondary trading is thin, financial risks cannot be properly priced, hedged, or shared with investors who are willing to carry them. Instead, those risks stay trapped on the balance sheets of commercial banks and local companies. 

Without a reliable bond market, banks take on dangerous timing mismatches between short-term deposits and long-term loans. Without active currency forward markets, businesses raise their prices to protect themselves against sudden exchange rate swings. Without deep stock markets, institutional investors stay away, and poor corporate management goes unpunished. At the same time, foreign direct and portfolio investors hesitate to commit capital, and regulators are left flying blind. Until we treat market liquidity as basic economic infrastructure, borrowing costs will remain high and our banking system will stay overburdened.

Fixed income: Loans dressed up as bonds

Consider the fixed-income market first. We often complain about our underdeveloped capital market, yet we eagerly celebrate the oversubscription of new corporate bonds and sukuk issues. Almost nobody pauses to ask who bought those bonds or whether they will ever trade. In reality, commercial banks buy the vast majority of these issues and lock them away until maturity. A bond that never trades in the secondary market is simply a bank loan in disguise. It does nothing to share risk outside the banking system or create a live market price for credit.

Today, Bangladesh's financial system still relies on commercial banks for roughly 80 per cent of all debt financing. Corporate bonds make up less than one-tenth of one per cent of gross domestic product, and secondary trading in corporate debt is almost non-existent. Even in government securities, where trading on Bangladesh Bank's electronic platform has grown, the market still lacks a continuous, reliable benchmark for long-term interest rates.

This gap creates serious problems for both borrowers and lenders. Suppose a mid-sized Bangladeshi manufacturer wants to build a factory that will take seven to ten years to pay off. The company cannot easily raise money by selling a ten-year fixed-rate bond to broad public investors. Large non-bank institutions, such as insurance companies and pension funds, refuse to buy long-term bonds that they cannot easily sell before maturity. As a result, the manufacturer must rely on bank financing whose interest rates change every six to twelve months. This leaves long-term business investments exposed to sudden interest rate hikes.

At the same time, commercial banks face a dangerous mismatch. Around 70 per cent of bank deposits mature within a single year, yet banks use these short-term funds to finance multi-year factory and infrastructure projects. Because banks cannot easily sell these loans or package them into tradable securities, they must hold every loan until it is paid off. When interest rates rise or the economy slows down, bank profit margins shrink rapidly. Worse, banks remain stuck with bad loans because there is no secondary market where distressed debt can be sold at a discount to specialized buyers.

Currencies: Hedging paralysis and higher prices

A similar bottleneck holds back our foreign exchange market. Bangladesh Bank has taken positive steps toward a more market-based exchange rate system. However, daily trading between banks is still concentrated in immediate spot deals and very short-term swaps. Longer-term forward contracts and currency hedging tools remain rare. Because commercial banks lack a deep secondary market to offset forward dollar commitments, they either refuse to offer forward contracts to mid-sized businesses or charge very high fees for them.

This inability to lock in future exchange rates directly fuels inflation and hurts exporters. An importer bringing in wheat, fertilizer, or industrial raw materials on a 90-day payment term cannot secure a fixed exchange rate in advance. To protect against a sudden drop in the Taka, the importer adds a large safety cushion to its local selling price. Ordinary consumers end up paying this hidden tax at the market.

Garment exporters face a similar squeeze. Many global buyers now take 90 to 120 days to pay for shipments. Traditional methods of matching export earnings against import bills no longer cover this time gap. Thin profit margins are left exposed to sudden currency swings. Furthermore, when dollar supplies tighten, the lack of continuous two-way trading encourages banks to hoard whatever dollars they hold. This widens the gap between buying and selling rates and delays international trade payments.

Equities: Trapped capital and weak governance

In the stock market, low liquidity harms both business innovation and corporate discipline. A strong stock exchange gives early-stage investors a reliable way to sell their shares once a company grows. Yet daily trading on the Dhaka Stock Exchange is often sluggish. Past regulatory measures, such as prolonged artificial floor prices that froze trading, are still fresh in investors' minds. Because of this, listing on the stock exchange no longer guarantees a smooth exit.

Global venture capital and private equity funds looking at promising Bangladeshi technology or logistics startups see this exit problem clearly. They either demand steep discounts on company valuations or insist that founders register their holding companies in Singapore or the United States before investing growth capital. Meanwhile, well-run local conglomerates avoid listing on the stock exchange altogether. They know that a market driven mostly by short-term retail speculation will not reward steady, long-term profit growth. As a result, top companies stay private, leaving public investors with fewer quality stocks to choose from.

Shallow trading also weakens corporate governance. In deep stock markets, large institutional funds hold company directors accountable. When a company mismanages money or ignores minority shareholders, institutional investors sell their shares in large numbers. This drives down the stock price, makes future borrowing more expensive, and puts pressure on company leadership to change.

In Dhaka, thin order books make it nearly impossible for a large fund to buy or sell a major stake without crashing the price against itself. Rather than getting trapped in stocks they cannot sell, institutional investors park their money in safe government treasury bills. Company sponsors face little market pressure to improve governance, and minority shareholders remain stranded.

Foreign capital: Why global investors stay on the sidelines

Weak secondary markets also explain why Bangladesh struggles to attract foreign portfolio investment and high-value foreign direct investment. Global asset managers evaluating emerging markets look closely at exit liquidity before investing a single dollar. Foreign portfolio investors need to know they can enter large positions in local stocks or government bonds, hedge their Taka exposure through liquid currency forwards, and repatriate funds smoothly without moving prices against themselves. When daily turnover is thin and currency hedging is unavailable, global funds simply exclude the market from their portfolios.

Foreign direct investors care about secondary market depth just as much. Multinational companies building factories, energy projects, or logistics hubs rarely fund their entire operations with foreign equity alone. They rely on local bond markets to raise long-term Taka debt, active currency markets to hedge imported machinery and dividend repatriations, and a credible stock exchange to list local subsidiaries over time. Without these secondary market supports, foreign direct investors face higher financing costs and trapped currency risk, driving them toward regional peers with deeper financial plumbing.

Demystifying AI finance: The supply chain, capital flows, and global rivalry

Regulators flying blind

Most critically, weak secondary markets leave financial regulators and policymakers flying blind. In mature economies, active secondary trading performs two vital public functions: real-time signaling and broad risk sharing. Continuous price movements in government bonds, corporate debt, and currency forward contracts act like a live dashboard. They warn officials about rising inflation expectations, cash shortages, or business stress long before those problems appear in monthly government statistics. Without these live market signals, central bankers and regulators must rely on outdated reports. As a result, policy decisions, such as interest rate changes or currency adjustments, often arrive too late, strike too early, or miss the true scale of the problem.

Equally damaging is the breakdown of risk sharing and market oversight. Deep secondary markets work like shock absorbers. They spread interest rate, currency, and credit risks across thousands of different investors, including insurers, pension funds, mutual funds, and foreign institutions. This broad participation also strengthens regulatory enforcement. In thin, fragmented markets, small groups can easily manipulate prices or trade on inside information without being noticed.

Until capital can exit our financial markets as easily as it enters, Bangladesh's financial system will remain a bottleneck rather than an engine for the next stage of economic growth

When risk is shared across a deep, transparent secondary market, abnormal price swings stand out immediately, helping regulators detect manipulation, curb insider trading, and enforce superior market governance. Without that depth, risk stays concentrated inside commercial banks, trapping authorities in a reactive cycle of emergency bailouts, loan forbearance, and blunt price controls that damage market trust even further.

The path to deeper, more resilient markets

Moving beyond empty slogans requires treating market liquidity as essential national infrastructure, just like ports, highways, and power grids. Policymakers and regulators must deliver five specific reforms.

First, authorities must modernize market technology and settlement plumbing. High transaction costs, fragmented platforms, and manual paperwork discourage frequent trading. Bangladesh needs unified, automated electronic order-matching platforms connected to central clearing counterparties and straight-through processing. Automating trade execution, custody, and settlement will lower transaction fees, speed up cash transfers, and give regulators real-time surveillance tools to flag insider trading and price manipulation automatically.

Second, regulators must permanently abandon artificial price controls. Floor prices on stocks and rigid caps on interest rates or exchange rates destroy market trust. Buyers and sellers must be allowed to discover true market-clearing prices without fearing that regulators will suddenly freeze their ability to exit.

Third, Bangladesh Bank should enforce genuine two-way market making. Licensed primary dealers in government bonds and authorized dealer banks in foreign exchange must be required to quote continuous, binding buy and sell prices throughout the trading day. To make this workable, the central bank should provide these market makers with dedicated short-term repo funding and clear hedging facilities.

Fourth, the government must remove tax and regulatory penalties on corporate bonds. Currently, high stamp duties, registration fees, and slow approval timelines make issuing a corporate bond far costlier and slower than taking a bank loan. Regulators should introduce fast-track shelf registration for credit-rated companies and give bond interest the same tax treatment as bank deposits.

Fifth, policy reforms must unlock long-term domestic savings alongside seamless foreign participation. Insurance companies, provident funds, and pension schemes hold vast pools of patient money, yet outdated investment rules restrict them mostly to fixed bank deposits and government savings certificates. Updating these rules, establishing an independent daily bond pricing agency, and simplifying custodial and currency repatriation rules for foreign funds will bring steady institutional depth to our markets.

Until capital can exit our financial markets as easily as it enters, Bangladesh's financial system will remain a bottleneck rather than an engine for the next stage of economic growth.

* Sajed ul Islam is a senior banking executive and financial markets specialist with three decades of global institutional experience across treasury, capital markets, and corporate governance.

item.title: Riyadh skyscraper damaged as Saudi reports new Houthi attacks
item.description:
A skyscraper in Riyadh housing the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund was damaged on Thursday, witnesses told AFP, as the kingdom reported new attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.

Saudi Arabia has been battling a surge in attacks since fighting reignited over the summer in neighbouring Yemen’s civil war, where Riyadh backs the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

In the early hours of Thursday, AFP journalists in the Saudi capital reported a powerful blast had been heard.

Around the same time, civil defence authorities issued a warning for “potential danger” but said minutes later that the danger had passed.

The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had “addressed a missile threat launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh”.

“Initial assessment indicates the impact of debris, with material damage currently being surveyed,” said coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki.

Witnesses later told AFP that Riyadh’s Public Investment Fund Tower, which at 80 storeys is the tallest in the city’s financial district, had been damaged.

“The facade is damaged across several floors, with windows blown out,” said one source who requested anonymity. Two other sources confirmed the damage.

Standing 385 metres high, the tower dominates King Abdullah Financial District, which acts as a showcase for Saudi Arabia’s economic ambitions.

With imposing skyscrapers, luxury shops and green spaces, the district also hosts the headquarters of the Saudi stock exchange along with multinationals such as Goldman Sachs.

Chaired by Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, the sovereign wealth fund is one of the largest in the world with more than $900 billion in assets under management.

It is also one of the main instruments for diversifying the kingdom’s economy away from oil, plans which have been threatened by the latest fighting.

Deadly airport attack

Malki also said Thursday that the coalition had intercepted five ballistic missiles launched towards Saudi Arabia’s southern region, which borders Yemen.

The Iran-backed Houthis have stepped up their attacks against Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, striking targets including airports, energy infrastructure, military sites and Riyadh’s financial district.

In October, a deadly attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 14 people and injured hundreds, forcing the suspension of flights for two weeks.

In response, the Saudi coalition has been striking Houthi targets in areas of Yemen held by the group.

On Thursday, Houthi media outlets reported that Saudi Arabia had launched another attack on Yemen’s capital Sanaa.

The Almasirah television channel said Saudi forces have “once again targeted the shoe and textile factory of the Alyateem Development Foundation”, citing its correspondent in Sanaa.

The Saudi coalition said it had “destroyed a ballistic missile launch platform in Dhamar”, a city about 100 kilometres (60 miles) south of Sanaa that was used by the Houthis to strike Riyadh.

Crown prince meeting

The long-running civil war in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, fell dormant in 2022 after a ceasefire was implemented, but sprang back to life this summer.

The Houthis are now nearing Aden, the internationally recognised government’s interim capital, having made sweeping territorial gains since the war resumed.

More than 1,600 people have been killed in the latest round of fighting and more than 300,000 displaced, according to the United Nations.

On Thursday, the Saudi crown prince met with US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh, according to state news agency SPA.

The two sides “reviewed bilateral relations, particularly in the military fields, and discussed regional developments”, the media outlet said.

On Wednesday, another powerful explosion rattled homes in Riyadh, with residents saying no mobile phone alerts were issued beforehand, as is usually the case.

“The explosion was extremely loud,” said one resident in the north of the city. “Hearing a blast without receiving a warning is very frightening.”

The coalition said it had intercepted two drones launched by the Houthis in the Riyadh and southern regions.

The military spokesman for the Houthis, Yahya Saree, said in a post on X that the group had targeted Riyadh’s international airport and the capital’s financial district with cruise missiles.

item.title: 20 factories in Gazipur, Savar declare holiday amid workers’ unrest, over 50 closed
item.description:
At least 20 garment factories in Gazipur and Savar, Dhaka, declared holidays on Thursday amid workers’ unrest. The authorities have also shut down more than 50 factories. Garment workers blocked the Dhaka–Mymensingh highway and staged protests in Gazipur on Thursday morning. Police later cleared the road. The situation in Savar remains calm so far.

Gazipur

Workers at several garment factories in the Mawna and Gorgoria Masterbari areas of Gazipur did not join work and staged protests on the Dhaka–Mymensingh highway on Thursday morning, demanding higher wages. Industrial police later removed them from the highway. Traffic movement along the road remained disrupted for around 20 minutes.

Meanwhile, workers from several factories attempted to stage a demonstration on the road in the Bhogra Bypass area along the same highway. Police also cleared the road there.

Authorities declared holidays at 10 garment factories in Gazipur on Thursday due to workers’ unrest. In addition, the authorities of more than 50 factories announced indefinite closures under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006.

Gazipur Industrial Police-2 Superintendent of Police Amzad Hossain said, “Incidents of workers’ unrest are still occurring sporadically in different areas today. Industrial police are working to keep the situation under control.”

Meanwhile, 13 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), five platoons of the Special Reserve Force (SRB) and 12 platoons of Ansar personnel remain deployed to ensure security in the Gazipur industrial zone. They are performing their duties in coordination with metropolitan, district and industrial police.

Gazipur Deputy Commissioner Nurul Karim Bhuiyan said, “Additional security measures have also been taken at Kashimpur Central Jail in Gazipur.”

Savar

Amid workers’ protests over various demands, including setting the minimum wage at Tk 30,000, a total of 29 factories in the industrial areas of Savar and Ashulia remained closed on Thursday. Another 10 factories declared general holidays for the day.

Workers at 17 factories reported for duty but did not work. BGB personnel, alongside police, are also performing security duties to maintain normal conditions.

Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, Superintendent of Police (SP) of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, confirmed the information at around 9:15 am on Thursday.

A visit to the Radio Colony, Ulail and Hemayetpur areas of Savar upazila on Thursday morning found that workers had arrived at various factories at their scheduled times. However, closure notices were displayed outside several factories near Padma Mor in Hemayetpur.

Khairul Mamun, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, told Prothom Alo, “The situation in Savar and Ashulia is much better today than on previous days. Workers at some factories are not working. However, the only effective way to maintain a peaceful and stable environment in the garment industry is to resolve the ongoing crisis by accepting workers’ legitimate demands, immediately releasing the arrested labour leaders and holding meaningful dialogue with the participation of all parties.”

Meanwhile, the Superintendent of Police of Ashulia Industrial Police-1 said, “Workers at a few factories have reported for duty but are not working. However, most factories are operating peacefully. So far, no reports of protests or instability have emerged from anywhere.”

item.title: Allegations of concealing toll collection information
item.description:
Allegations have been raised of revenue evasion by concealing the actual information on toll collection on the Dhaka Elevated Expressway. According to the allegations, the foreign investor company is reporting fewer vehicles than the actual number using the elevated expressway.

There are also allegations of assigning toll collection responsibilities to a third party without authorisation, dismissing Bangladeshi employees and demoting them.

Sources concerned said that the Special Branch (SB) of police submitted a report to the Bridge Division on 3 September regarding these allegations, seeking action. Although the Bridge Division has denied the allegations, it said that a separate mechanism would be introduced to monitor toll collection.

The Dhaka Elevated Expressway is a major public-private partnership (PPP) project. According to the agreement, if daily vehicle traffic exceeds 80,000 for 15 consecutive days, the Bangladesh government will receive 25 per cent of the revenue generated from tolls on the additional vehicles.

If daily vehicle traffic falls below 13,500, the operating company will receive a subsidy. Allegations have been raised that although more than 100,000 vehicles currently use the expressway daily, no revenue is being paid to the government.

However, according to information provided by the investor company, 70,000 to 75,000 vehicles currently use it each day.

Project director Golam Mortuza also referred to the same figures for vehicle traffic. He said he had recently joined and was unaware of the allegations of irregularities.

The Dhaka Elevated Expressway PPP project is overseen by the Bangladesh Bridge Authority (BBA). First Dhaka Elevated Expressway Company Limited (FDEE) is responsible for its construction, operation and maintenance.

Initially, Thailand-based Italian-Thai Development held more than half of the shares, but after disputes among partners reached the court, its shareholding dropped to 1 per cent.

Currently, China Shandong International Economic and Technical Cooperation Group holds 80 per cent of the shares, while Sinohydro Corporation holds 19 per cent.

After 25 years, the investors will hand over the elevated expressway to the Bangladesh government. Before that, they will recover their invested money, including interest, through toll collection.

The SB report said that a confidential investigation found that approximately 100,000 vehicles use the expressway daily. However, to show the actual number as below 80,000, toll information for some vehicles is not being entered into the central software or digital system, and tolls are being collected manually.

There are also allegations of collecting tolls during busy hours without issuing online receipts and reusing the same receipt for multiple vehicles.

A spot inspection found that during busy hours, employees stand with tickets in hand in various lanes alongside the toll booths. The registration numbers of vehicles receiving these tickets do not appear on the electronic boards.

Bridge Division Secretary Mohammad Abdur Rouf told Prothom Alo that over the three years since the expressway opened, vehicle traffic had exceeded 80,000 on a total of 21 days, but not consecutively. The government will receive revenue only if the number exceeds that threshold for 15 consecutive days.

He said records were also being maintained for vehicles paying tolls manually or through conventional methods. Saying that he was not calling the SB report “wrong,” he said the report had expressed suspicion. They would look into whether toll collection was being carried out properly.

When contacted, FDEE Administration Manager Siang Shweinan said that since the project authority is the BBA, anyone seeking information on any matter should discuss it with them through the BBA.

Third-party responsibility and employee layoffs

After the expressway opened, incidents of robbery and bodies being dumped there took place. Criminals took advantage of the absence of CCTV cameras in some locations.

Without resolving these problems, last year FDEE engaged another Chinese company named Shandong Hi-Speed International Operation and Maintenance Private Limited in toll collection as well as operation and maintenance work.

Over the following year, Bangladeshis holding various senior positions at FDEE were removed and Chinese nationals were appointed in their place. Demotions and dismissals also took place. Before Eid-ul-Azha last year, nine Bangladeshi employees were dismissed.

Sajib Rahman (30), a dismissed lane assistant, told Prothom Alo that the day before Eid, a driver paid Tk 100 against a toll of Tk 80 and drove away. He did not keep the remaining Tk 20 and threw it into a dustbin.

However, he was dismissed over the allegation of “keeping the money.” Eight others like him were also dismissed on the same allegation.

Employees allege that they were not informed when they were transferred from FDEE to Shandong Hi-Speed. In March last year, the company obtained a trade licence from the government. Later, a Chinese official of the company asked them to provide all toll collection information.

The employees claim that under the PPP agreement, FDEE is responsible for collecting tolls. BBA approval is required to assign this responsibility to another company. However, such approval was not obtained.

A review of BBA correspondence shows that on 13 September, the BBA wrote to FDEE seeking to know the legal status of Shandong Hi-Speed. In its reply on 28 September, FDEE said that although Shandong Hi-Speed had obtained separate registration, it had not been formally assigned responsibility for operation and maintenance.

FDEE alone was carrying out these responsibilities. However, in a letter dated 29 October last year, Shandong Hi-Speed described itself as a contracted operation and maintenance company working with FDEE.

According to the SB report, Shandong Hi-Speed is collecting tolls without proper approval. The company’s office was not found at the North Badda address it had provided to BIDA (currently the Invest Bangladesh Authority). It is operating from FDEE’s address in Kuril. No information about this was found to have been provided to BIDA, nor was any separate agreement with the BBA found.

The report also contains allegations of failure to renew the trade licence, non-compliance with labour laws and the ratio of local and foreign employees, and several foreign nationals not having valid work permits.

Bridge Division Secretary Abdur Rouf said that the investor company could appoint anyone it deemed suitable for toll collection. He expressed hope that once construction up to Kamalapur is completed by June next year, vehicle traffic and government revenue would increase.

Call for effective monitoring

The project, undertaken in 2009, began construction in 2020. The 19.73-kilometre expressway, costing approximately Tk 90 billion, is supposed to extend from Kawla, south of the airport, to Kutubkhali.

According to the agreement, the investor company is bearing 73 per cent of the construction cost of the main structure, while the government is bearing 27 per cent. After several extensions, the latest deadline has been set for December 2028. The section from the airport to Farmgate opened in September 2023.

Adil Muhammad Khan, professor of the Department of Urban and Regional Planning at Jahangirnagar University and executive director of the Institute of Planning and Development, said there had been complaints about the project for a long time.

Bangladesh’s interests had not been adequately protected in the agreement. Although the investor’s financial investment had been accounted for, the monetary value of the land provided by the government and the rehabilitation costs had not been taken into consideration.

He said effective government monitoring was essential regarding how many vehicles were using the expressway and how tolls were being collected.

The SB report should be taken into consideration and action should be taken, and officials who violated the country’s interests in the project should be held accountable. He advised exercising caution in protecting the country’s interests when undertaking PPP projects in the future.

item.title: Banned Chhatra League holds procession with machetes, oars near BNP MP’s house in Chattogram
item.description:
Leaders and activists of the banned Chhatra League held a procession carrying machetes and logi-boitha (bamboo poles and oars) near the house of BNP (Bangladesh Nationalist Party) Member of Parliament (MP) Sarwar Jamal Nizam in Anwara, Chattogram.

The incident took place on a road in the Toiladwip area of Barkhain Union in the upazila on Wednesday night.

According to local sources, the house of MP Sarwar Jamil Nizam is only 100 metres from the spot where the procession took place. All the participants in the procession were wearing helmets. After the procession, they poured petrol on the road and set it on fire. They then left the area.

A 2.38-minute video of the procession went viral on social media on Thursday morning. The name of banned Chattogram South District Chhatra League leader Robiul Haider and the organisation’s logo can be seen in the video.

It shows 20 to 25 young men gathering on the road wearing helmets and masks, pouring petrol and setting it on fire. Some of them were carrying sticks and logi-boitha, while others were carrying machetes.

Officer-in-Charge of Anwara police station Md. Junaet Chowdhury confirmed the procession.

He said, “We have seen a video of the procession. In the name of holding a procession, they attempted to create disorder by cutting down trees. We have detained two people on suspicion of involvement in the incident. The others are being identified by examining the video, and necessary legal action is being taken.”

item.title: 96 platoons of BGB deployed in 7 districts, with drones, body-worn cameras
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) has deployed 96 platoons across seven districts to maintain law and order and ensure public security.

The districts where BGB personnel were deployed on Thursday are Dhaka, Gopalganj, Narayanganj, Gazipur, Faridpur, Mymensingh and Chattogram. Another five platoons of BGB personnel remain on standby for deployment.

A BGB press release issued on Thursday confirmed the information.

According to the release, BGB deployed 23 platoons in Dhaka, 15 in Chattogram, six in Narayanganj, 15 in Gazipur, 27 in Gopalganj, two in Mymensingh and three in Faridpur.

The press release stated that the BGB personnel, deployed on the instructions of the Ministry of Home Affairs, were carrying out their duties in coordination with the respective district administrations and other law enforcement agencies.

BGB said it had strengthened security and surveillance at key installations, industrial zones and various other locations in the districts concerned. Its personnel were also working to prevent disorder, violence and any activities that could threaten public safety.

According to the press release, the BGB headquarters' monitoring cell was maintaining technology-based surveillance to closely monitor and coordinate operations on the ground.

For this purpose, the cell was continuously monitoring live video footage transmitted through drones, body-worn cameras and improvised devices.

BGB said that, alongside their regular border duties, its personnel were performing their responsibilities in the districts concerned with the utmost professionalism, discipline and patience.

The force also said it was taking necessary precautionary measures to ensure the safety and security of the public and their property, maintain uninterrupted movement and daily activities, and respond to any unforeseen situation.

item.title: RUET announces admission test date; 18,000 students to get chance to sit exam
item.description:
RUET announces admission test date; 18,000 students to get chance to sit exam

Correspondent,

The admission test for the first-year undergraduate programme at Rajshahi University of Engineering and Technology (RUET) for the 2026–27 academic session will be held on 28 January next year. 

This time, the examination will be held at two centres — RUET and Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) — using a common question paper.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the steering committee for RUET’s first-year undergraduate admission test on Wednesday afternoon (18 November). 

The university’s Vice-Chancellor, Professor SM Abdur Razzak, was present at the meeting. It was chaired by Professor Md Kamruzzaman, dean of the Faculty of Civil Engineering and chairman of the admission test steering committee. 

RUET disclosed the information in a press release.

According to university sources, the admission test will be held in the multiple-choice question (MCQ) format. Of the applicants who meet the preliminary eligibility criteria, 18,000 students will be selected on merit to sit the examination. The test will be held for more than 1,200 seats at RUET.

To be eligible to sit the admission test, candidates must have passed the Secondary School Certificate (SSC) or an equivalent examination in 2023 or 2024, with a minimum GPA of 4. They must also have passed the Higher Secondary Certificate (HSC) or an equivalent examination in 2026. 

Their combined GPA in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry at the HSC level must be at least 13, with a minimum GPA of 4 in each subject.

Specific eligibility criteria have also been set for students who have passed the GCE O-Level and A-Level examinations. They must have obtained at least a B grade in a minimum of five O-Level subjects and at least a B grade separately in Mathematics, Physics and Chemistry at A-Level. They must also have received their A-Level certificates in November 2025 or later.

Professor Md Kamruzzaman, chairman of the admission test committee, told Prothom Alo that candidates meeting the required eligibility criteria based on their secondary and higher secondary examination results would be able to apply. 

However, submitting an application would not automatically guarantee a place in the admission test, he added. “The top 18,000 applicants would be selected on merit to sit the examination.”

Kamruzzaman further said the decision to hold the admission process in January had been taken in consideration of a court injunction. The date had also been set with a view to avoiding potential clashes with admission tests at other universities, so that students would not face difficulties.

Meanwhile, the university’s Public Relations Office said further decisions regarding other aspects of the admission test would be taken at subsequent meetings of the steering committee.

item.title: Actress Jyotika Jyoti detained at midnight
item.description:
It was nearly 2:45 am. Police had gathered outside the residence of actress Jyotika Jyoti in Uttara, Dhaka. Even before they entered, the actress went live on Facebook, breaking down in tears. She insisted she had no involvement in any wrongdoing and pleaded with officers not to put her in handcuffs. 

Finally, the Detective Branch (DB) of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) detained her in the early hours of Thursday (19 November).

Jyotika Jyoti was taken into custody from a residential apartment in Sector 18 of Uttara, under the jurisdiction of Turag police station. Md Mostafizur Rahman, Officer-in-Charge of the police station, confirmed the news to Prothom Alo.

According to Mostafizur Rahman, the actress was arrested at around 2:45 am and taken to the DB office on Minto Road for questioning.

However, the police official could not immediately confirm which specific case she would be shown arrested under. 

Various media outlets have reported that she was detained over allegations of maintaining links with leaders and activists of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned in the country.

Facebook live ahead of detention

After police arrived at her residence, Jyotika Jyoti went live on Facebook multiple times, appearing tearful while several police officers stood outside her front door.

During the live broadcast, the actress claimed she had no idea why the police had come to her home or why she was being detained. At one point, she stated, "The police have come to arrest me without a warrant. I am not involved in any wrongdoing."

Addressing the police personnel, Jyoti added, "Had you simply called me, I would have gone to the police station or the DB office myself. Please do not put handcuffs on me. I am coming with you."

Towards the end of the broadcast, the actress sought to reassure her parents, saying, "I am not afraid. Ma, Baba (parents)—please do not be afraid."

Controversy over ‘Alo Ashbei’ WhatsApp group

Following the fall of the Awami League government in the student-led mass uprising on 5 August 2024, a WhatsApp group named “Alo Ashbei” drew widespread scrutiny. In September of that year, screenshots of conversations from the group leaked on social media.

The leaked exchanges featured several actors, journalists, and cultural figures making disparaging remarks about the Anti-Discrimination Student Movement and the protesters, sparking fierce public criticism. Jyotika Jyoti’s name was among the members of that group.

At that time, the actress had come onto Facebook Live to clarify her position, claiming the group’s intention was never to harm the country or its people, and that she merely shared updates regarding the situation in Dhaka during the protests.

She had also remarked that no artist could ever support the killing of human beings.

Dismissal from Shilpakala Academy

Following the Alo Ashbei group controversy, Jyotika Jyoti also faced professional fallout. In 2023, she was appointed on a contractual basis as Director of the Research and Publication Department at the Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy.

After the change of government on 5 August 2024, Jyoti stayed away from her workplace for several days. When she eventually returned to the Shilpakala Academy on 17 September, she faced protests from a section of her colleagues, who opposed her over her involvement in the Alo Ashbei group and her stance against the protesters. She was eventually forced to leave the premises.

On 30 September of that year, her contractual appointment was cancelled via a notification issued by the Ministry of Public Administration—a development that came to light the following day.

Sharing a photograph of the official gazette on Facebook, Jyoti noted that it marked the end of her first government job.

In July 2026, an organisation filed a complaint at the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) against 28 cultural and media personalities,  including Jyotika Jyoti, over alleged crimes committed during the mass uprising.

Whether her current arrest is linked to that complaint remains unclear.

Over 2 decades in acting

Jyotika Jyoti began her journey in the entertainment industry in 2004 through a beauty pageant, later establishing herself as a regular presence in both television dramas and films.

Her notable films include Ayna, Nondito Noroke, Rabeya, Jibondhuli, Anil Bagchir Ekdin, Maya: The Lost Mother, and Lal Moroger Jhuti.

Beyond Bangladesh, Jyoti has also acted in cinema made from India’s West Bengal. She played the role of Rajlakshmi opposite Kolkata actor Ritwick Chakraborty in Pradipta Bhattacharyya’s Rajlakshmi O Srikanta, adapted from Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay’s classic novel.

Born in Gouripur, Mymensingh, Jyotika Jyoti gravitated towards unconventional roles from the outset of her acting career, remaining active in cultural initiatives alongside drama and film.

In a career spanning more than two decades, the actress has drawn public attention for various reasons—now finding herself back at the centre of debate following her midnight arrest from home.

item.title: The people of Bangladesh and Portugal have much in common, Princess Maria Francisca says
item.description:
There are many similarities between the lifestyles, cultures and values of the people of Bangladesh and Portugal. Greater interaction between the two countries could create opportunities for people to learn a great deal from one another.

In particular, European countries need to know more about the abilities and skills of the people of Bangladesh.

Princess Infanta Maria Francisca, a member of Portugal’s Royal House of Braganza (Bragança), made these remarks while visiting the Prothom Alo office in Karwan Bazar, Dhaka, on Wednesday. Her husband, Duarte de Sousa Araújo Martins, accompanied her. Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman welcomed them.

The members of Portugal’s royal family are visiting Bangladesh at the invitation of London Tea Exchange. As part of their visit, they toured the Prothom Alo office on Wednesday.

Officials of London Tea Exchange said one of the main objectives of the visit was to promote Sylhet tea in the international market. They are also involved in initiatives to strengthen cultural and trade relations between the people of the two countries and ensure fair wages for tea workers.

The discussion meeting at the Prothom Alo office covered the historical ties between Bangladesh and Portugal, similarities in language and culture, migration, the potential of the tea industry and the social role of the media.

Others attending the meeting included London Tea Exchange Group Chairman Sheikh Aliur Rahman, Director Abdul Mohammad Shalim Mukit, UK-based lawyer Farhan Khan Farani and journalist Mohammad Tahir Chaudhry, among others. Senior members of the Prothom Alo team also took part in the discussion.

Princess impressed by Bangladesh’s hospitality

At the beginning of the meeting, Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman highlighted several words of Portuguese origin used in the Bengali language. He said many words used in everyday Bengali had similarities with Portuguese. He cited the words ‘girja’, ‘padri’, ‘kamra’ and ‘alkatra’ as examples.

Princess Maria Francisca said, “It is truly remarkable. It is a wonderful experience to learn that the languages of the two countries have so much in common.”

The Princess also observed that the two countries shared similarities in their food habits and social customs, in addition to their languages.

Maria Francisca said, “We Portuguese love gathering around a large table filled with food and sitting together. We spend hours eating, talking and chatting. I can see the same culture in Bangladesh. Last night, as I sat down for dinner, I felt as though I was attending a dinner in Portugal.”

Sharing her experience of visiting Bangladesh, Maria Francisca said, “What I have liked most about Bangladesh is its people. Their warmth and hospitality are truly remarkable.”

Maria Francisca said, “The people of Bangladesh are highly capable and skilled. Unfortunately, their abilities are not properly recognised, particularly in many European countries, including Portugal. More people around the world need to understand the true value of the people of Bangladesh, their culture and their potential.”

The discussion also touched on Bangladeshis living in Portugal. Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman spoke about their lifestyles and the various challenges they face there.

In this regard, Maria Francisca said that negative perceptions of Bangladeshis were sometimes created in Portugal. However, she noted that many Bangladeshis were hardworking and skilled people with a very rich culture.

At this point, the Princess’s husband, Duarte de Sousa Araújo Martins, said another major similarity between the people of Bangladesh and Portugal was that both had spread across different parts of the world.

The Portuguese had travelled to and settled in various countries for a long time, and the same could be seen among Bangladeshis.

Historical ties between Portugal and Bangladesh

Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman also highlighted the historical ties between Bangladesh and Portugal. He said the history of contact between the two countries went back a long way.

Recalling his visit to Portugal, Matiur Rahman said he had travelled to Lisbon, the country’s capital, in 1979 to attend an international conference in support of Palestine.

During his four- to five-day stay, he met several prominent Portuguese figures, including Álvaro Cunhal, then General Secretary of the Portuguese Communist Party.

Matiur Rahman said they had followed with keen interest the fall of authoritarian rule in Portugal in 1974 and the independence of several African countries, including Angola, Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau.

In this connection, Princess Maria Francisca said the independence of African countries had been a very significant development. However, she noted that Portugal had simply left those countries behind.

After independence, Portugal should have done more to help them develop the necessary infrastructure and state institutions.

Maria Francisca added, “We must acknowledge that many wrongs and injustices took place in the past. However, longstanding relations also led to the development of family, social and cultural ties among different communities. That history cannot be completely denied.”

Praise for Prothom Alo’s social initiatives

Prothom Alo Head of Marketing Azwaj Khan briefed the guests on the newspaper’s activities at the discussion meeting. Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman explained that the newspaper began its journey in 1998.

Alongside its news coverage, the organisation had worked from the outset in education, healthcare, women's rights and the development of disadvantaged communities.

He highlighted the long-standing initiatives of the Prothom Alo Trust, including running schools in remote areas, providing scholarships to underprivileged students and campaigning against acid attacks on women.

Praising these initiatives, Princess Maria Francisca said, “You have done some remarkable work over the years. You truly deserve the recognition you have received. In particular, you are giving a voice to those who are not usually heard.”

The Princess particularly praised Prothom Alo’s educational initiatives. She said it was extremely important to create opportunities for children in remote areas to learn about the world beyond their familiar surroundings and to dream big.

Discussion on media freedom

At one point during the discussion, the participants addressed media freedom. Mohammad Tahir Chaudhry, a Pakistani journalist based in the UK and editor of Urdu Times, asked what kind of pressure Prothom Alo faced in Bangladesh regarding press freedom and the right to information.

In response, Matiur Rahman said Prothom Alo had faced various forms of pressure and adversity under successive governments in Bangladesh.

There had also been pressure during the previous 16 years of government, as well as various challenges under the subsequent interim government. However, he expressed hope that the situation would improve to some extent in the coming days.

International initiative to promote Sylhet Tea

During her stay in Bangladesh, the Princess is scheduled to visit various areas, including Sreemangal, and several tea gardens. One of the main objectives of her visit is to express support for the Global Fair Pay Charter, an international initiative aimed at ensuring fair wages for tea workers.

The discussion also covered the potential of Bangladesh’s tea industry. Prothom Alo Editor Matiur Rahman said, “Although Darjeeling and Ceylon tea are well known around the world, high-quality tea from Bangladesh has yet to gain similar recognition in the international market.”

He also highlighted the poor living conditions of tea workers and stressed the need for initiatives to ensure fair wages and improve their standard of living.

At this point, London Tea Exchange Group Chairman Sheikh Aliur Rahman said the organisation was launching a brand called “Sylhet Tea” to promote tea from

Sylhet in the international market. The initiative has historical ties with Portugal’s Royal House of Braganza ((Bragança)).

Sheikh Aliur Rahman further said that “Sylhet Tea” had already been introduced in Portugal. Around 14 countries across the world had expressed interest in sourcing the tea.

item.title: Saboteurs’ targets now include state installations
item.description:
Activists of the Awami League, whose activities have been banned in the country, and banned Chhatra League attacked Tungipara police station in Gopalganj on Tuesday and set it on fire. Eight police vehicles and eight motorcycles were burned in the fire. Seven police personnel were injured in the attack. They are now receiving treatment at a hospital.

The incident of setting fire to Tungipara police station in Gopalganj is not the only one. Earlier, incidents of crude bomb explosions had taken place targeting Pallabi police station in Dhaka and the office of the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of the police.

Sources concerned say saboteurs are targeting important state installations. In the coming days, they are planning attacks on police stations and important state installations. They also have plans to disrupt road and water transport communications.

Police say security has been strengthened at important state installations. Security has also been increased on highways.

As of Tuesday, over 11 days, arson attacks had been carried out on 57 vehicles and crude bombs had exploded at 70 locations across the country. Thirty-five cases have been filed in connection with these incidents. Sixty people have been arrested.

According to police information, these acts of sabotage took place across the country from 7 to 17 November. During this period, a police vehicle was damaged in a cocktail bomb explosion. In addition, crude bombs were exploded at two police installations.

Today, a text message from the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) said that police had arrested 71 members of the Awami League, whose wactivities in the country are banned, over the past 24 hours. They were arrested on allegations of involvement in sabotage.

Police Headquarters spokesperson Assistant Inspector General (AIG) Kamarum Munira told Prothom Alo that if anyone, in the name of programmes organised by a banned organisation, attempts to deteriorate law and order, disrupt public safety, engage in sabotage or violence, or obstruct public movement, the police will take necessary measures in accordance with the prevailing law.

The police official said that, considering the possible situation surrounding the programme, police intelligence surveillance and security preparedness would be in place.

A senior police officialDeploying more police, BGB and SRB would not help either. This is because saboteurs know that members of law enforcement agencies will not fire.

Police would remain alert to protect people’s lives and property as well as public and private assets. However, police would also be mindful to ensure that no innocent person is harassed. At the same time, police would ensure the highest level of professionalism in carrying out their duties.

Men of Awami League, whose activities banned, set Tungipara police station on fire

Increased preparations surrounding the lockdown

Police sources said preparations had been made in view of the nationwide “lockdown” programme announced by the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned in the country, for Thursday. Additional police would be deployed to maintain security across the country, including Dhaka.

Block raids and checkpoint operations have been intensified. Security has been strengthened at the entry points to the capital. Long-distance buses are being searched.

Incidents of vehicles being set on fire and crude bombs being exploded by people arriving on motorcycles have been taking place. Therefore, motorcycles moving around the capital are also being searched.

During a visit to the capital on Wednesday, checkpoints were seen set up in the Badda, Rampura and Hatirjheel areas, where long-distance buses, passengers’ bags and motorcycles were being searched.

Operations at Tungipara police station suspended after vandalism, arson
BNP MP Jilani’s house set on fire in Tungipara as attackers chant ‘Joy Bangla’

Several police officers on duty at the checkpoints told Prothom Alo that they were working to prevent anyone from carrying out sabotage ahead of the lockdown programme.

Police have recovered more than two kilograms of gunpowder from a leader of the banned Chhatra League in the Mirpur area of the capital. Police say the gunpowder had been brought to Dhaka from Meherpur for sabotage.

A senior police official, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said that despite deploying 2,000 police personnel, 10 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) and SRB in Gopalganj, the police station had still been attacked.

Deploying more police, BGB and SRB would not help either. This is because saboteurs know that members of law enforcement agencies will not fire, he said.

He added that importance was being given to collecting advance intelligence and increasing checkpoints to tackle sabotage.

Regarding preparations surrounding the lockdown programme, Dhaka Metropolitan Detective Branch chief Shafiqul Islam said adequate measures had been taken to ensure the safety of Dhaka residents in view of the lockdown programme announced by the banned Awami League.

Intelligence surveillance had been increased. Additional police would be deployed. Block raids and checkpoint operations were underway. Police were prepared to prevent any kind of disorder and chaos.

The DB official said that the promotion of various programmes on social media was also being taken seriously. Their authenticity was being verified, and necessary measures were being taken to prevent them.

Police have recovered more than two kilograms of gunpowder from a leader of the banned Chhatra League in the Mirpur area of the capital. Police say the gunpowder had been brought to Dhaka from Meherpur for sabotage.

What the police are considering to tackle sabotage

Sources concerned said saboteurs were attacking police installations and police personnel in an attempt to force them to fire. But the government is talking about alternatives to firing.

Police have suggested to the government that the situation be handled politically or through the presence of party leaders and activists. At the same time, the police are focusing on ensuring that state installations are not attacked. They are also prioritising bringing those directly involved in sabotage swiftly under the law.

A senior police official, speaking to Prothom Alo on condition of anonymity, said that despite deploying 2,000 police personnel, 10 platoons of BGB and SRB in Gopalganj, the police station had still been attacked. Deploying more police, BGB and SRB would not help either.

This is because saboteurs know that members of law enforcement agencies will not fire, he said. He added that importance was being given to collecting advance intelligence and increasing checkpoints to tackle sabotage.

Gunpowder had been brought to Dhaka from a border area of Meherpur to plan arson and sabotage in various locations, including Mirpur in the capital. The DB says a central leader of the banned Chhatra League was coordinating the operation through WhatsApp.

A police source said a large amount of money was being spent on sabotage by former ministers and members of parliament who are fugitives abroad, as well as leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations. They are now working to stop the flow of funds for sabotage.

In a district, police officials held a meeting in the presence of a minister with leaders and activists of the BNP and its affiliated organisations regarding the recent situation.

Addressing the police, they said that during the Awami League government, whenever BNP leaders and activists gathered somewhere, police would arrive at the scene within five minutes. Why were police now unable to do so?

A senior district police official then said that previously, leaders and activists of the Chhatra League and Jubo League would be present on the ground and help police by providing information. Now police were not receiving any information from BNP leaders and activists.

Gunpowder brought from Meherpur

Gunpowder had been brought to Dhaka from a border area of Meherpur to plan arson and sabotage in various locations, including Mirpur in the capital. The DB says a central leader of the banned Chhatra League was coordinating the operation through WhatsApp. Three people, including a Chhatra League leader, have been arrested in the case. A total of 2 kilograms and 290 grams of gunpowder were recovered from them.

These details were disclosed by DB chief Shafiqul Islam at a press conference at the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) Media Centre on Mintoo Road in the capital on Wednesday afternoon.

The arrested individuals are Mamun Or Rashid (27), a former student of the Management Department at Islamic University and joint convener No. 1 of Chhatra League; Ibrahim Hossain Moon (50), an executive member of the Awami League and former president of the Rajshahi University Chhatra League unit; and Meghla Milli (41), a Jubo League leader. The process of taking legal action against the arrested individuals is underway.

Shafiqul Islam said intelligence agencies had received information that an organised group was planning sabotage with the aim of destabilising the country. Citing information obtained during interrogation, he said Mamun had stated that he had collected gunpowder from a border area through a Chhatra League office-bearing leader in Meherpur for the purpose of setting fire to various government and private installations in Dhaka, including Mirpur, carrying out sabotage and creating panic among the public.

He later brought the gunpowder to Dhaka through a Mirpur Chhatra League leader for delivery to Ibrahim Hossain and Meghla Milli. A central leader of the banned Chhatra League was coordinating the operation through WhatsApp.

item.title: PM leaves for Lalmonirhat on daylong visit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left here for Lalmonirhat this morning to join three programmes in the northern district.

The premier departed Tejgaon Airport by a helicopter at 9:15 am, said PM’s Additional Press Secretary Atikur Rahman Rumon.

He will join three programmes and return to Dhaka in the afternoon, Rumon added.

During the visit, the Prime Minister will attend the first National Aero-Genius Competition, organised by the Aviation and Aerospace University Bangladesh, as chief guest. He will also visit the university campus.

He will also inaugurate the re-excavation of the Mahendranagar drainage canal in Sadar upazila and exchange views with the local beneficiaries.

Later, he will join a programme titled “Alokito Lalmonirhat” (Enlightened Lalmonirhat) at the district Collectorate Ground.

Tarique Rahman last visited Lalmonirhat about 22 years ago as a BNP leader. This is his first visit to the district as Prime Minister.

item.title: Crude bombs explode at 3 Dhaka locations at night, truck set ablaze
item.description:
Crude bombs (locally known as cocktail) exploded in the capital’s Shahjahanpur, Shyampur and Sher-e-Bangla Nagar areas, while miscreants set fire to a truck in Mohammadpur. 

Four people, including a woman, were injured in the incidents. Police detained one person. The incidents took place between Wednesday evening and midnight.

The first cocktail explosion occurred at around 6:30 pm in front of Khilgaon Government Primary School, beside Khilgaon Railgate Kitchen Market in Shahjahanpur.

Amirul Islam, officer-in-charge (OC) of Shahjahanpur police station, told Prothom Alo that miscreants had thrown a crude bomb from the Khilgaon Flyover. It exploded on the road, seriously injuring a nearby tea-stall owner, Nasima Begum. She was admitted to Mugda Medical College Hospital.

Later, at around 8:40 pm, two crude bombs exploded in front of the Dolairpar bus counter in Shyampur.

Mohammad Nazrul Islam, OC of Shyampur police station, said a man named Hridoy had been caught red-handed in connection with the incident. He was taken to the police station. Details about his identity and alleged involvement in the explosions were not yet available.

At around 10:00 pm, another crude bomb exploded in front of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, injuring three more people.

Muhammad Shahidul Islam, OC of Sher-e-Bangla Nagar police station, told Prothom Alo that one of the injured had been sent to Dhaka Medical College Hospital, while the other two received primary treatment at Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital. 

Police were working to identify those responsible for the explosion, he added.

Later, at around 11:30 pm, a parked truck was set on fire in front of a truck stand in Dhaka Udyan, Mohammadpur. Local residents tried to put out the fire.

Abdul Halim, OC of Mohammadpur police station, told Prothom Alo that the truck parked in front of the stand had been set on fire. 

He suspected that the incident might have stemmed from a dispute with someone associated with the stand.

The Mohammadpur police station OC further said seven security guards were present at the site. They initially believed that outsiders would not have had an opportunity to set fire to the truck. Police are investigating the incident.

2 arrested over bomb explosions

Police have arrested two activists of the banned Chhatra League and Jubo League while they were allegedly preparing to carry out crude bomb attacks in the Bashundhara and Uttarkhan areas of the capital.

The Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) disclosed the information in a media release.

According to the release, law enforcement from Bhatara police station arrested Mohammad Dipu Talukdar, 21, former vice-president of the Dhaka North city unit of Chhatra League, from Bashundhara Residential Area. He was arrested at around 6:15 pm. Two live crude bombs wrapped in adhesive tape were recovered from his possession.

Police also arrested Jubo League leader Robiul Islam, 30, over his alleged involvement in a crude bomb attack in Uttarkhan. He was arrested from the Helal Market area at around 7:30 pm. He is a member of Ward 45 of the Dhaka North city unit of Jubo League.

Police said a group of 25 to 30 people had thrown a crude bomb at the house of a certain Ripon Hossain in the Ojapara area of Uttarkhan at around 6:45 pm last Tuesday. The bomb struck the wall beside the entrance to the house and exploded.

Subsequently, acting on intelligence, police obtained information about Robiul Islam’s alleged involvement in the incident and arrested him.
