item.title: Bus, goods-laden truck set on fire in Narayanganj
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to a passenger bus and a straw-laden truck at two separate locations in Narayanganj on Thursday morning.
No casualties were reported.
The incidents took place near Kanchpur Bridge on the Dhaka-Chittagong Highway and at Mirertek Bazar on the Asian Highway.
According to police and local sources, a Tisha Paribahan passenger bus was set on fire on the Dhaka-bound lane near Kanchpur Bridge at around 9:30am. All passengers managed to get off the bus immediately after the fire broke out. However, the bus was extensively damaged.
Kanchpur Highway Police Station Officer-in-Charge Jewel Mia said the damaged bus was removed from the scene using a recovery vehicle. No one was injured in the incident, he added.
Photo: Dhaka Tribune
In a separate incident, a straw-laden truck parked near Mirertek Bazar was set on fire early Thursday.
The truck, carrying straw from Dinajpur, stopped in front of Mirertek Bazar Jame Mosque at around 3:30am. The driver and helper parked beside the road while waiting to unload the cargo and fell asleep inside.
At around 5:30am, a woman passing by noticed the fire and alerted the driver. He tried to extinguish the flames by throwing the burning straw into water beside the road.
Police reached the scene after receiving the information and alerted the Fire Service. A Fire Service team brought the blaze under control at around 7:30am. By then, all the straw on the truck had been destroyed.
Jasim Uddin, in-charge of the Taltala police outpost, said the truck's cargo was destroyed in the fire, but the driver and helper were unharmed.
Those involved would be identified and brought to justice, he added.

item.title: Around 20 factories in Gazipur declare holiday amid workers' unrest
item.description:
Around 20 factories in Gazipur have declared a holiday for Thursday amid ongoing workers' unrest, although the Industrial Police reported closures at five garment factories in Sreepur and the Bhogra Bypass area.
The closures were announced in phases from 8:15am, according to police.
Meanwhile, in the Ansar Road area of Sreepur, leaders and activists of different units of the BNP’s municipal branch, led by its Member Secretary Billal Hossain Bepari, were seen taking positions along the highway and in nearby areas to prevent possible sabotage or unrest.
Police and local residents said workers at Mondol Intimates in the Bagher Bazar area arrived at the factory in the morning and registered their attendance but did not start work. Shortly after 8:15am, they left the premises without management’s permission.
After leaving the factory, the workers gathered at the gate of Golden Refit Garments on the western side of the highway, prompting workers at that factory to come out as well.
The workers then gathered on the highway and demanded the closure of other factories, prompting several establishments in the area to declare a holiday.
Among them were Silken Sewing, Esrotex Garments Ltd in the Notun Bazar area, SM Knit Wear Ltd, Subline Green Tex of Meghna Group in the Sreepur Municipality-Aspada area, Chittagong Denim Ltd in the Gargaria Masterbari area and Meghna Garments.
The workers later moved in groups from Gargaria Masterbari towards Sreepur.
Authorities also declared holidays at around 20 factories along the same road and in nearby areas. These included Crystal Garments, Demimec Garments, Divine Garments, Dhaka Fashion Ltd of Hams Group, Victoria Intimates, Takwa Fashion and Takwa Poshak Kalakan of Palmal Group, the Sustainable Wet Processing Plant, and Meghna Denim and Uniglory Washing Ltd.
Asked about road blockades, Sreepur Upazila Assistant Commissioner (Land) Nahid Niyaz Shishir said the situation had persisted for the past three weeks, with sporadic blockades reported at different locations, including Bangla Bazar in Rajendrapur, Hotapara and Gargaria Masterbari.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amjad Hossain said workers arrived at factories in the morning, registered their attendance and then left without starting work.
He said police intervened when workers later attempted to block the highway towards Sreepur and cleared the road. The situation had since returned to normal.
However, he said authorities had declared holidays at five factories in the Sreepur and Gazipur areas.
A deputy general manager of a garment factory in Bagher Bazar, requesting anonymity, said workers from a neighbouring factory gathered at his factory's gate. As they began pushing against the gate, the management decided to send its own workers home.

item.title: 96 BGB platoons deployed in 7 districts
item.description:
A total of 96 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel have been deployed in seven districts to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and respond to any untoward incidents.
The deployment covers Dhaka, Chittagong, Narayanganj, Gazipur, Gopalganj, Mymensingh and Faridpur.
Of the total, 23 platoons have been deployed in Dhaka, 15 in Chittagong, six in Narayanganj, 15 in Gazipur, 27 in Gopalganj, two in Mymensingh and three in Faridpur. Another five platoons are on standby for deployment.
In a statement on Thursday, BGB said its personnel were operating in coordination with the respective district administrations and other law enforcement agencies, following instructions from the Ministry of Home Affairs.
BGB personnel are strengthening security and surveillance at key installations, industrial zones and other important locations to prevent disorder, violence and activities that could threaten public safety, the statement said.
The BGB headquarters' monitoring cell is also maintaining technology-based surveillance to closely monitor and coordinate the situation on the ground.
Live footage from drones, body-worn cameras and improvised devices is being monitored round the clock, the statement added.

item.title: Tarique reaches Lalmonirhat on daylong visit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman reached Lalmonirhat by helicopter on Thursday morning on a daylong visit to attend several programmes in the northern district.
He landed at Lalmonirhat Airfield around 10:30am, said his Deputy Press Secretary, Jahidul Islam Rony.
Disaster Management and Relief Minister and Lalmonirhat-3 MP Asadul Habib Dulu, Chief of Air Staff Air Chief Marshal Hasan Mahmood Khan, and senior officials of Rangpur Division and Lalmonirhat district welcomed him.
During the visit, Tarique is scheduled to attend the first National Aero-Genius Competition organised by Aviation and Aerospace University, Bangladesh, as the chief guest and visit the university campus.
He will then inaugurate the re-excavation of a drainage canal at Mahendranagar in Lalmonirhat Sadar upazila and exchange views with local beneficiaries.
After a brief stop at Lalmonirhat Circuit House, the prime minister will attend a program titled "Alokito Lalmonirhat" at the district Collectorate Ground.
He is scheduled to return to Dhaka by helicopter on Thursday evening.

item.title: Five burned in gas leak fire at Kathalbagan
item.description:
Five people were burned in a fire caused by a suspected gas leak at a residential building in Kathalbagan, Dhaka, on Thursday morning.
The injured were admitted to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery, where three of them are in critical condition.
The fire broke out on the fourth floor of the 10-storey Kanchan Tower in Kathalbagan at around 8:20am on Thursday.
According to the Fire Service media department, two units from the Mohammadpur Fire Station rushed to the scene after receiving the report and began efforts to control the fire.
The blaze was brought under control at 8:45am.
Dr Sultan Mahmud Sikdar, resident surgeon (emergency) at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery, said five burn victims were brought to the institute for treatment, three of whom were in critical condition.

item.title: Fire breaks out at Rayerbazar kitchen market
item.description:
A fire broke out at the Rayerbazar kitchen market and several tin-roofed houses beside it in Dhaka on Thursday morning.
The fire started at around 10:20am on Thursday and was brought under control at 10:55am with the efforts of four Fire Service and Civil Defence units.
According to the Fire Service and Civil Defence Media Cell, two units each from the Hazaribagh and Mohammadpur fire stations were dispatched to the scene after receiving reports of the fire. The units arrived at around 10:35am and began working to bring the blaze under control.
The cause of the fire and the extent of the damage could not be immediately determined.
No casualties were reported, the Fire Service said.

Miscreants set fire to Gazipur Palli Bidyut complaint centre
item.description:
Miscreants set fire to a pile of old wooden materials inside a complaint centre at the Gazipur Palli Bidyut Samity office early Thursday.
The fire broke out at around 3:30am on Thursday at the complaint centre in the Bhurulia area of Gazipur city after two containers of petrol were thrown inside.
Ziaul Haque, deputy general manager of Gazipur Palli Bidyut Samity, said fire service personnel rushed to the scene after receiving the information and brought the fire under control.
Two containers were recovered from the scene. However, it is too early to determine whether they contained petrol or were used in a sabotage attempt without further investigation, he said.
Mohammad Raja Mia, an inspector at Gazipur Fire Service, said three units of the Joydebpur Fire Service brought the fire under control after an hour of efforts.
Old electricity poles and wooden transformer boxes were damaged in the fire.
Aminul Islam, officer-in-charge of Gazipur Metropolitan Police's Sadar police station, said police visited the scene after receiving reports of the incident.

item.title: Panchagarh records season's lowest temperature at 12.5°C
item.description:
Winter is beginning to set in across Panchagarh, with the minimum temperature dropping to 12.5°C on Thursday, the lowest recorded in the district this season.
The Tetulia Weather Observation Centre recorded the temperature at 6am, with relative humidity at 98%.
The minimum temperature fell by 3.2°C in a day, from 15.7°C recorded at 9am on Wednesday.
According to the weather observation centre, the minimum temperature was 17.4°C on Tuesday, 18.5°C on Monday, 16.4°C on Sunday, 15.8°C on Saturday and 15.7°C on Friday. The maximum temperature on Wednesday was 27.6°C.
Local residents said the weather remains warm during the day due to sunshine, but temperatures drop after sunset.
Jitendranath Roy, acting officer-in-charge of the Tetulia Weather Observation Centre, said temperatures may gradually fall further in the coming days.
A mild cold wave may sweep through Panchagarh in December, he added.

item.title: Khulna BNP leaders detain, hand over two youths to police after arson incident
item.description:
Two youths were detained by Khulna district BNP leaders and handed over to police after allegedly setting fire to an area in Gallamari under Labanchara police station in Khulna on Thursday morning.
The detainees were identified as Koushik, 21, and Yasin, 22.
BNP leaders and activists caught the two youths near Labanchara police station while they were fleeing the scene after setting fire. They were later handed over to Labanchara police station.
Khulna district BNP Convener Moniruzzaman Montu, Member Secretary SM Monirul Hasan Bappy and other party leaders and activists were present during the handover.
Labanchara police station Officer-in-Charge Syed Mosharraf Hossain said the two youths were kept in police custody after receiving preliminary medical treatment.
They are being questioned over the incident, while police are investigating whether others were involved, he said.
Further legal action in the case is underway, the OC added.

item.title: Satkhira-Dhaka bus services suspended over security concerns
item.description:
Long-distance bus services on the Satkhira-Dhaka route via the Padma Bridge have been suspended amid fears of road blockades and violence in Gopalganj.
The suspension took effect on Wednesday afternoon, with transport operators confirming that no buses would leave Satkhira for Dhaka on Thursday.
According to transport counter officials, several buses left for Dhaka via the Padma Bridge on Wednesday morning. However, services were suspended from the afternoon following reports of road blockades and unrest at various locations in Gopalganj.
A limited number of buses are operating via an alternative route through Jessore and the Paturia-Daulatdia ferry terminals.
Swadhin, manager of Imad Paribahan's Patkelghata counter, said no buses would operate on the route on Thursday due to security concerns.
Zahir Raihan, manager of SK Paribahan's Satkhira counter, confirmed the suspension, saying drivers, workers and transport owners were concerned following incidents of vehicle arson in different parts of the country.
The sudden suspension has left passengers travelling to Dhaka for urgent work in difficulty. Passengers said alternative routes were increasing both travel time and inconvenience.
Transport operators said services via the Padma Bridge would remain suspended until the situation returned to normal and the administration ensured adequate security.
Bus services from Khulna to Dhaka have also been suspended over the same incident.

item.title: July uprising memorial torched, crude bombs exploded in Tangail
item.description:
Vandals set fire to a memorial dedicated to those killed during the July uprising in Mirzapur upazila of Tangail on Wednesday night.
The incident took place beside the Gorai Highway Police Station, near the Dhaka-Tangail-Jamuna Bridge Highway.
Several crude bombs also exploded near the Gorai flyover and surrounding areas around the same time, triggering panic among locals.
No casualties were reported.
Locals said the vandals set fire to the July uprising martyrs' memorial beside the Gorai Highway Police Station at around 11:30pm. A few minutes later, several crude bombs exploded in succession beneath the Hatur Bhanga flyover in Gorai before the perpetrators fled.
The memorial was completely gutted before police and fire service personnel could reach the scene.
The incident has heightened tensions in the Gorai area.
It is suspected that activists of the Awami League may have carried out the attack ahead of the party's announced lockdown program for Thursday, despite the party's activities being banned.
Mirzapur police station Officer-in-Charge Abdullah Al Mamun said police from Mirzapur and Gorai Highway Police stations rushed to the scene after receiving the information and brought the fire under control.
He added that law enforcement agencies have been conducting regular patrols over the past few days along the Dhaka-Tangail-Jamuna Bridge Highway, the Gorai industrial area, Mirzapur upazila headquarters and other key locations to prevent sabotage.
Police are working to arrest those involved, he said.

item.title: Two BRTC buses torched, railway track set on fire in Rajshahi
item.description:
Vandals set fire to two parked buses at the Bangladesh Road Transport Corporation (BRTC) bus terminal in Rajshahi city and torched a section of railway tracks in Charghat upazila.
Both buses were gutted in the fire at the BRTC terminal in the Am Chattar area under Shah Makhdum police station.
Shah Makhdum police station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Md Akbar Ali confirmed the incident, saying the fire broke out at around 2:25am on Thursday.
According to police, miscreants set fire to the two buses parked at the terminal. Fire service personnel rushed to the scene and brought the blaze under control.
Akbar Ali said police were deployed at the scene immediately after the incident. No one has been arrested in connection with the incident so far.
Meanwhile, a section of railway track was set on fire in Bagmari village under Nimpura Union of Charghat upazila in Rajshahi at around 11:15pm on Wednesday.
Train services on the route remained suspended for an hour before resuming. Locals jointly brought the fire under control after the perpetrators fled.
The Dhaka Commuter train, travelling from Dhaka to Chapainawabganj, was stranded at the affected section.
A team from Charghat Model Police Station headed to the scene after receiving the report. Railway authorities at the local station were also informed to check for any damage to the tracks or technical faults.
Ahmed Hossain Masum, general manager of Bangladesh Railway's Western Zone, said the fire was set in the Bagmari area, east of Nandangachhi Railway Station in Charghat, at around 11:15pm. Train services resumed at 12:05am on Thursday.

item.title: How ancient philosophy became modern self-help
item.description:
"O jar apon khobor apnar hoy na
ekbar apnare chinte parle re jabe achenare chena.”
In other words, someone who does not know their own self may come to know what once seemed unknown by learning who they really are.
Lalon Fakir sang those lines in Kushtia, in a mud hut, without formal schooling or scripture to guide him, and without any apparent need to convince anyone of anything. He was not setting out to write philosophy. He was putting an insight into words, as village songs often do, and somehow arrived at something a Roman emperor would write down in a war tent and a Greek slave who became a teacher would repeat to his students: Know yourself first, and the rest begins to make sense.
That, really, is what this article is about. We tend to think that wisdom about how to live is something new, something we find in a bestselling book or pick up from a fifteen-minute TED Talk. But most of these questions are much older than the labels we give them.
Bauls sang about them on the roads of Kushtia, philosophers debated them in gardens outside Athens, and an emperor wrote about them between battles, long before anyone thought to call this kind of advice “self-help.”
Mark Manson makes a similar point in his essay “Why We All Need Philosophy,” where he argues that we need a way of thinking suited to the problems of modern life. Look closely at today’s self-help culture and you can see what he means: It often circles back to conclusions philosophers reached thousands of years ago, only with better marketing.
Take Cal Newport’s Deep Work , which urges us to protect our attention from distraction. Seneca was making a related point long ago when he observed that people guard their money carefully but throw away their time, “the one thing in which it is right to be stingy,” as though it costs them nothing.
James Clear’s Atomic Habits makes the case that our identity shapes our behaviour. Epictetus had already put the idea plainly: “First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do.”
Sharon Lebell brings the same spirit to The Art of Living: The Classical Manual on Virtue, Happiness, and Effectiveness , her modern rendering of Epictetus. At the heart of the Stoic teaching is a simple distinction: Some things are within our control, and some are not. Much of our suffering begins when we fail to tell the difference.
That idea was written down when Rome was still an empire. Today, it sits close to the heart of an industry that sells us advice on how to live.
Living in the age of statistics
Today, almost everything can be tracked, measured, optimized, or tested against something else.
We know our sleep scores, our step counts, and how many minutes we have spent looking at a screen. We can measure a remarkable amount about our lives, sometimes down to the smallest detail. And yet all that information does not necessarily tell us whether we are living well. For all the numbers we collect, many of us still feel unsure about where we are going.
Compare that with the philosophers of antiquity. They did not have our devices or data, but they spent a great deal of time asking a question we still struggle with: What does it actually mean to live well?
Epicurus, who is often mistaken for a champion of indulgence, argued for something closer to radical simplicity. He wrote: “It is possible to provide security against other ills, but as far as death is concerned, we men live in a city without walls.”
He was not asking people to outrun death by staying busy or gathering more possessions. He was asking them to look clearly at what matters and what does not.
“If you wish to be rich, do not add to your money, but subtract from your desires.” It is hard to think of a more direct challenge to a culture that keeps telling us we need one more thing before we can be satisfied.
What the ancients knew that we keep relearning
A few ideas recur across the schools of ancient philosophy, and they sound remarkably familiar beside the advice filling the self-improvement shelves today.
Marcus Aurelius, the philosopher-emperor, wrote what could almost pass for an early productivity mantra: “You have power over your mind -- not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.”
Long before Deep Work , the underlying point was already there: You cannot control everything happening around you, but you can pay attention to how you respond.
Seneca argued that a life without hardship leaves a person untested. He compared it to a fighter who has never taken a real hit. What we now call grit, he understood as a part of character: something that is formed, in part, by having to face difficulty.
Epictetus put it this way: “Make the best use of what is in your power, and take the rest as it happens.” The idea resembles what we now call locus of control: Knowing where your effort can make a difference, and learning not to spend all your energy on what lies beyond it.
None of these similarities is especially surprising. Our tools have changed far more than our basic human worries. We have built rockets and neural networks, but we still wake up anxious about things we cannot control.
And we still need someone, whether a Stoic teacher who was once enslaved or a productivity YouTuber, to remind us to sit down and do the next right thing.
Philosophy is not complicated
Somewhere along the way, philosophy became a university subject rather than a way of living. It was wrapped in dense texts, footnotes, and academic language, then put behind the doors of departments that often struggle to attract students.
Philosophy was never meant to stay inside a lecture hall. It belongs in that brief moment before you lose your temper and say something you cannot take back.
Epictetus made much the same point to his students nearly 2,000 years ago. For him, philosophy was not something to admire from a distance. He urged his followers not to stop at learning, but to put what they learned into practice and keep training themselves.
Returning to the question
We live in a culture that measures value by output. Time is something to spend efficiently, a person is something to optimize, and even learning is treated as an investment that must pay a return. In this logic, a question earns its place only if it produces something.
Questions that cannot be priced, such as what makes a life good or what we owe one another, do not disappear. They simply lose their place, or never occur to us at all, because the world gives us no reason to look for them.
What follows is a habit of passive consumption. We take in advice, trends, and ready-made formulas for success, and we rarely stop to examine them. The meaning of a good life is defined for us by markets, media, and the people around us, and we adopt it without asking whether it is ours.
Philosophy was not refuted. It was crowded out by busyness, and by the belief that reflection is a luxury for when the work is done. Epicurus warned against dismissing philosophy in just this way:
“He who says either that the time for philosophy has not yet come or that it has passed is like someone who says that the time for happiness has not yet come or that it has passed.”
The self-help industry is not wrong to return to habits, focus, resilience, and meaning. The problem is that it can make old questions look like brand-new discoveries.
Perhaps the next step is not to buy another book, but to return to a practice that the Stoics made time for at the end of the day: Asking yourself what you did well and what you could do better.
Not to punish yourself for getting things wrong, but to learn. You would practice any skill you wanted to improve, so why should living well be any different?
Sharif Al Zubayer Zishan is an aspiring writer and journalist.

item.title: Tigresses exit Emerging Nations Trophy despite win over Thailand
item.description:
Bangladesh Women's cricket team have been eliminated from the ICC Women's Emerging Nations Trophy despite securing a narrow three-run victory over Thailand in their final group-stage match at Ajman today.
Bangladesh finished level on four points with Zimbabwe in the group but missed out on a place in the Super Six due to an inferior net run rate.
Zimbabwe secured qualification after defeating the Netherlands by 33 runs.
Batting first after losing the toss, Bangladesh struggled early and lost both openers cheaply. Nigar Sultana Joty and Sharmin Akhter attempted to rebuild the innings, with Nigar scoring team-best 45 off 36 balls and Sharmin contributing 16.
Stand-in captain Sobhana Mostary added a valuable 28 off 26 deliveries as Bangladesh posted 132-6 in the stipulated 20 overs.
In pursuit of the 130-run target, Thailand faced early pressure as Bangladesh's Sanjida Akhter Meghla claimed two wickets. However, Nannapat Koncharoenkai and captain Naruemol Chaiwai revived the chase with a 52-run partnership for the third wicket.
Nannapat top-scored with 57, while Naruemol contributed 33 as Thailand remained in contention until the closing stages.
Thailand needed 21 runs from the final two overs but ultimately managed to put up 129-5, falling three runs short of Bangladesh's target.
Despite the victory, Bangladesh's narrow winning margin proved insufficient to improve their net run rate enough to overtake Zimbabwe, bringing their campaign to an end at the group stage.

item.title: Climate risk is financial risk
item.description:
Since the adoption of the Paris Agreement on December 12, 2015, climate change and its impact on the economy, industrialization, commerce, and trade have gained importance in policy formulation and the sustainable development agenda.
An important aspect of the agreement, particularly relevant to the financial sector, is Article 2.1(c), which calls for making financial flows consistent with a pathway towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development. This provision gives climate considerations a wider significance beyond environmental protection and places the alignment of financial resources with climate objectives within the broader framework of sustainable development.
Although the Paris Agreement does not prescribe guidance for individual lending decisions for commercial banks, its objectives provide an important policy direction for governments, regulators, and financial institutions.
As a signatory to the agreement, Bangladesh has also shifted its policy toward a low-carbon economy, and its banking sector has received new guidelines on sustainable finance -- including climate finance -- to build a climate-resilient economy.
The sustainable finance department (SFD) of Bangladesh Bank has progressively strengthened its policy framework for sustainable finance and climate-risk management. The department has also offered refinance schemes at lower interest rates to encourage banks and financial institutions to ensure the flow of funds into climate-friendly, low-carbon-emitting industrial establishments .
The economic cost of climate vulnerability
The German based Global Climate Risk Index ranked Bangladesh as the 13th most climate vulnerable country in 2026. The World Bank’s Country Climate and Development Report for Bangladesh (2022) identifies tropical cyclones, flooding, rising sea levels, extreme heat, and other climate-related hazards as significant threats to the country's development effort.
The report estimates that average tropical cyclones alone cost Bangladesh approximately$1 billion annually. It also warns that climate variability and extreme events could cause the loss of one-third of agricultural GDP by 2050. Under severe flooding scenarios, economic output could fall substantially below projected levels. The report further estimates that 13.3 million people could become internal climate migrants over the coming decades if climate impacts on agriculture, water availability, and coastal areas intensify.
In the World Bank report, An Unsustainable Life: The Impact of Heat on Health and the Economy of Bangladesh, it was said that Bangladesh's maximum temperature had increased by approximately 1.1°C since 1980, while the perceived temperature had risen by around 4.5°C. Heat-related health conditions and productivity losses resulted in an estimated 250 million lost workdays in 2024, with an economic cost of up to$1.78 billion, equivalent to approximately 0.4% of GDP.
These figures are very concerning for the banking sector. When economic activity is disrupted, borrowers' repayment capacity can deteriorate. A factory facing repeated production interruptions may experience declining revenue and rising operating costs. The consequences can appear in a bank's financial statements as increased overdue loans, higher credit impairment, reduced collateral values, and greater provisioning requirements.
Climate change affects financial performance of businesses, changes asset value, and disrupts supply chains, ultimately affecting the repayment capacity of the borrower. A flood can damage a factory, communication system, cause labour displacement which ultimately interrupts production, affect revenue and earnings. Salinity can affect agricultural output and the availability of freshwater. A cyclone can destroy infrastructure, disrupt transportation, supply chain, and deteriorate the cash flow of businesses.
These are not merely environmental consequences that can be considered temporary. They can directly affect a bank’s credit portfolio, earnings, and provision requirements.
These risks affect banks’ operations and credit portfolio in multiple ways depending on the borrower’s location, industry concentration of credit portfolio, business model, and capacity to adapt.
For example, a readymade garment manufacturing company located in an area exposed to recurrent flooding may have a sound financial position, however, repeated floods may damage machinery, interrupt production, increase insurance costs, and delay the delivery of export orders. This event may eventually affect its ability to service debt.
Enactment of new laws relating to carbon emission, environment protection, technological developments, market preferences, and investor expectations are principal sources of transition risk which can also affect the competitiveness and profitability of businesses.
More importantly, transition risks must be addressed from a global perspective. The ready-made garment sector is facing different carbon related regulations imposed by the buyers which forces them to consider upgrading environmental performance, energy efficiency, resource consumption, and sustainability standards. A factory that fails to invest in cleaner production, energy efficiency or improved environmental performance may face higher operating costs or lose business opportunities.
The transition to a low-carbon economy creates challenges, but it also generates investment opportunities. Renewable energy, energy-efficient industrial equipment, green buildings, cleaner production technologies, business automation, and sustainable transportation are areas where banks can play a significant financing role.
The gap between policy and credit decisions
Despite the introduction of regulatory guidelines and various sustainable finance initiatives by the central bank, an important implementation challenge remains: T ranslating climate-risk considerations into routine banking and credit decisions. B anks still treat climate change as an environmental and development issue, largely outside the conventional responsibilities of commercial banks.
In conventional credit appraisal, banks generally place considerable emphasis on the borrower's financial statements, projected income, cash-flow adequacy, debt-servicing capacity, profitability, leverage, collateral coverage, repayment history, and overall business prospects. Project financing decisions also rely on financial viability assessments and capital budgeting techniques.
These remain essential elements of sound lending. Social and environmental concerns including climate risk is addressed through regulatory clearances, environmental permits, and environmental and social due d iligence (ESDD).
Climate-risk assessment requires a broader perspective. It raises additional questions: Is the borrower's business located in an area exposed to recurrent flooding or extreme heat? Does the business depend heavily on water or other climate-sensitive resources? Could changes in environmental regulations or buyer requirements affect its competitiveness? Does the borrower have adequate measures to protect its assets and maintain business continuity? Most importantly, how could these vulnerabilities affect future cash flows, collateral values, and repayment capacity?
These are the questions that need to become part of the credit assessment process, particularly for sectors and geographical locations with significant climate exposure. To address all these issues, climate-risk considerations should become part of the bank's overall credit risk framework and must be considered as an integral part of risk governance.
The importance of climate stress testing
One of the most important tools to address climate risk is the climate stress testing. Banks can incorporate climate components and effects of their variability on income and asset value of the borrower in risk assessment metrics. Stress testing models can be designed to assess the impact of climate risk parameters on individual client level as well as to assess climate risk on the overall portfolio of the bank based on loan segregation on industries and concentration to different areas.
A useful approach to conduct climate stress testing should be to identify material climate-sensitive sectors, map portfolio exposure by geographical location and sector, assess the vulnerability of borrowers, and examine how different climate scenarios could affect their financial performance. The resulting analysis may help banks identify concentrations of risk that are not readily visible through conventional portfolio reporting.
However, climate stress testing to address climate risk at portfolio level as well as at individual borrower level in Bangladesh is not that easy to conduct overnight. It has practical challenges.
Reliable borrower-level location data, detailed climate projections, sector-specific vulnerability information, flood and rainfall related historical data, and suitable analytical models are not yet available across the market. Bangladesh Bank can take an initiative to develop a model for climate related stress testing.
Banks should therefore adopt a phased approach. Initial assessments can use available geographical and sectoral information, followed by progressively more sophisticated models as data quality and institutional capacity improve. At the initial stage, banks can introduce climate-risk screening into the credit appraisal process.
Adaptation finance: The overlooked aspect of climate finance
It is now evident that in most cases, banks use their resources in climate finance to mainly focus on climate risk mitigation -- particularly renewable energy, energy efficiency, installation of effluent treatment plants (ETP) aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emission. These investments remain important.
Mitigation finance supports activities that reduce or avoid greenhouse gas emissions while adaptation finance is very crucial to manage livelihoods of the most vulnerable communities.
However, for a climate-vulnerable country like Bangladesh, adaptation finance deserves equal attention. Adaptation finance supports investments that help businesses and communities prepare for and recover from climate-related impacts.
Examples include flood-resilient industrial infrastructure, improved drainage systems, rainwater harvesting, water-efficient irrigation, climate-resilient agricultural practices, improved storage facilities, saline-tolerant crop varieties, and climate-resilient infrastructure.
These investments may not always generate immediate financial returns in the conventional sense but their value often lies in preventing future losses, protecting productive assets, and maintaining business continuity.
The reason that the banks are not engaging more actively in scaling up adaptation finance is that the communities affected by climate change generally live far away from the banks. Moreover, economic vulnerability and financial fragility of the affected community, difficulties to identify bankable adaptation projects, uncertainty of financial return and repayment capacity, and a lack of technical knowledge to assess climate risk are also obstacles for banks to engage in adaptation finance.
What the banks can do
Considering the socio-economic importance of adaptation finance, banks must come forward with some practical market-oriented approach to address the issue.
Banks may be encouraged to set up specialized branches in climate-vulnerable areas where the staff shall be dedicated for selecting viable projects addressing the local adaptation needs.
For example, an agricultural enterprise could consider investments in water-efficient irrigation, improved drainage, climate-resilient storage, and other adaptation measures.
Similarly, financing a manufacturing company in a flood-prone area could include investment in flood protection, improved electrical infrastructure, elevated machinery, and business continuity arrangements.
Banking networks like sub-branch or agent banking outlets can be used to expand banking activities in remote climate sensitive areas. This will also reduce cost and help ensure financial inclusion and affinity with the local communities.
Banks should also invest in staff development. Relationship managers need to understand basic climate exposure and adaptation opportunities. Credit analysts need to know how climate-related factors may affect cash flow, collateral, and repayment capacity. Risk management teams need the capability to analyze portfolio concentration and conduct scenario-based assessments.
NGO-linked adaptation finance
One particularly promising approach for Bangladesh may be to establish an NGO- l inked climate adaptation finance m odel. This approach can address several barriers simultaneously, particularly discovering bankable projects, lack of collateral, high transaction costs, and limited access to vulnerable communities.
Under this arrangement, a commercial bank can provide wholesale financing to qualified NGOs, which subsequently extend adaptation financing to their existing beneficiaries. Banks need to develop special schemes and reporting guidelines for NGOs.
Policy support from central bank
It is not possible for commercial banks alone to address all the barriers independently. A supportive regulatory and institutional environment is necessary to encourage adaptation lending. The c entral bank must come forward with some initiatives. Moreover, rules regarding loan loss and provision requirements ought to be relaxed for climate finance exposure.
Understanding the nature of the investment
There is a fundamental distinction between commercially - viable adaptation investments and adaptation activities that primarily generate public benefits.
Consider the construction of climate - resilient infrastructure like a coastal ban k. This cannot be a commercial project. Banks should not be expected to finance every adaptation requirement through conventional loans schemes.
Projects that produce substantial social and economic benefits but require long payback and grace period s may require grants, government funding, or concessional blended finance. Mandatory climate risk f unds preserved by the commercial banks can be a good source of financing for projects of public interest.
Climate finance should not be viewed merely as an additional compliance obligation or a form of concessional lending. It should be recognized as a strategic credit risk management instrument. By financing adaptation measures today, banks can reduce the probability of future borrower distress, protect the quality of their loan portfolios, and contribute to the long-term resilience of the economy.
C limate finance therefore should not be treated simply as a reporting category or a numerical target. Banks need to develop commercially viable products that respond to the actual investment requirements of businesses.
Shakhawat Ahmed Khan is a banker by profession. Email: khan.shakhwat@gmail.com .
